reference.source: GeneReviews / Smith's Recognizable Patterns of Human Malformation
clinicalPearls: An X-linked duplication of the Xq28 region that includes MECP2, affecting males, while carrier females are usually unaffected because of skewed X-inactivation
Infantile hypotonia, feeding difficulty and delayed motor milestones with absent or very limited speech
Recurrent respiratory and other infections, reflecting associated immune dysfunction, are a major cause of morbidity and early death
Progressive neurological deterioration with developmental regression, worsening spasticity and, in many, epilepsy
Autistic features and severe to profound intellectual disability are characteristic
Represents a gain-of-function dosage effect of MECP2, in contrast to the loss-of-function of the same gene that causes Rett syndrome in girls
The rearrangement is typically inherited from an unaffected carrier mother, with important recurrence-risk implications for male relatives
Chromosomal microarray is the first-line diagnostic test and defines the duplication extent
reference.pathophysiology: MECP2 duplication syndrome results from a gain of an extra copy of the MECP2 gene at Xq28, usually within a larger duplication of variable size; some rearrangements are recurrent and mediated by non-allelic homologous recombination between segmental duplications in this repeat-rich region. MECP2 encodes a methyl-CpG-binding protein that regulates transcription of many neuronal genes, and both excess and deficiency of the protein disrupt neurodevelopment. Overexpression produces progressive neurological dysfunction, hypotonia evolving to spasticity, and an immune phenotype predisposing to recurrent infection. Because the gene is X-linked, males with a single X are affected, whereas carrier females with favourably skewed X-inactivation are typically spared.
additionalDifferentials: Rett syndrome and other MECP2 loss-of-function disorders (chiefly in females)
Cerebral palsy and other causes of progressive spasticity with developmental delay
Mitochondrial and neurometabolic disorders presenting with regression
Primary immunodeficiency presenting with recurrent infection and developmental delay
Other causes of infantile hypotonia with global developmental delay
additionalInvestigations: Chromosomal microarray as first-line to detect and size the Xq28 duplication
FISH or MLPA to confirm the duplication and to test the mother for carrier status
Maternal and family studies to identify carriers and counsel recurrence risk in males
Immunological assessment given the susceptibility to recurrent infection
EEG and brain MRI where seizures or regression are present
Respiratory, swallowing and developmental assessment with surveillance for aspiration
redFlags: Recurrent or severe respiratory infection with risk of respiratory failure
Developmental regression or loss of previously acquired skills
Aspiration or feeding difficulty threatening nutrition and airway safety
reference.prognosis: The condition is generally severe and progressive, with profound intellectual disability, loss of independent mobility and a significant risk of premature death, frequently from recurrent respiratory infection. Attentive respiratory care, infection prevention, seizure management and nutritional support can improve comfort and reduce complications, but the overall outlook remains guarded.
pitfalls: Failing to test the mother and female relatives for carrier status, given the important recurrence risk for future sons
Overlooking the immune dysfunction and underestimating the risk of severe recurrent infection
Confusing the gain-of-function duplication with the loss-of-function mutations that cause Rett syndrome
Attributing regression to a static encephalopathy and missing the progressive nature of the disorder
references: Smith's Recognizable Patterns of Human Malformation
Emery and Rimoin's Principles and Practice of Medical Genetics
